name: Breaking the feedback loop
description: Use CBT to examine a concern once, then metacognitive techniques to disengage from repetitive analysis. The goal is to respond proportionately to reality and return attention to your life, not to eliminate unwanted thoughts or change your values.
review: Repetition is not evidence. Emotional intensity is not accuracy.
Separate facts from interpretations. Examine a concern once and identify any practical action.
I do not need resolution to disengage. Reopen an issue only when there is new evidence or a genuine reason to reconsider it.
A thought is not an obligation to think. Notice it and return attention to what I was doing.
Reality is my validation dataset. Test assumptions through real experiences. Learn from mistakes without repeatedly examining them.
Delay emotionally charged responses. Give nonurgent consequential decisions and confrontations 24 hours without rehearsing arguments. Act sooner if safety or a real deadline requires it.
Practise attention control for five minutes. Focus on one sound for two minutes, switch between sounds for two minutes and notice several sounds together for one minute.

reports.name: Daily rumination check-in
reports.description: Take about two minutes. Focus on what happened in your day, not on analysing the thoughts themselves.

questions.label: How much did repetitive thinking interfere with my day?
labels: I was distracted but did what I intended

questions.label: How easily could I disengage from repetitive thinking today?
Did I act impulsively on amplified emotions?
Did I practise five minutes of voluntary attention control?
Which skills did I practise today?
options: Returned attention to a concrete activity

reports.name: Weekly feedback loop review
reports.description: Take around five minutes. Look for patterns in your behaviour, not new explanations of old thoughts.

questions.label: How much did repetitive thinking interfere with my life this week?
labels: I was distracted but did what I intended

questions.label: How consistently did I recognise repetitive thinking before it escalated?
Did I handle workplace, relationship or other disagreements more proportionately?
What did I learn from one real-world observation or behavioural experiment?
questions.hint: One or two sentences. Record new evidence or an outcome, not another interpretation.

questions.label: Which skill will I prioritise next week?

reports.name: Monthly progress review
reports.description: Take five to ten minutes. Review completed reports if helpful. A partial first month is fine. Assess the effect on real life rather than analysing every thought.

questions.label: How much did repetitive thinking interfere with my life this month?
labels: I was distracted but did what I intended

questions.label: Where have I noticed a practical improvement?
options: Time and attention for meaningful activities

questions.label: What concrete change in my behaviour or daily life shows progress or a remaining difficulty?
questions.hint: One or two sentences about observable behaviour.

questions.label: What one practical adjustment will I make next month?
questions.hint: One action, not a new theory. This can be continuing a useful practice or seeking professional support.
